question: The granting of Spanish nationality to Cuban regime-linked individuals and Schengen security risks under Spain’s ‘Ley de Nietos’

According to press reports1, the US Department of State is examining the granting of Spanish nationality under Spain’s Democratic Memory Law (’Ley de Nietos’) to individuals linked to the Cuban regime and allegedly connected to Caribbean drug trafficking and transnational organised crime.

Spanish judicial reporting2 has also stated that the Ministry of Justice granted nationality to former Venezuelan deputy minister Nervis Villalobos, amid alleged pressure linked to a corruption network, as investigated by the Guardia Civil’s central operational unit.

At the same time, Portugal has moved in the opposite direction, tightening access to nationality, and is considering its withdrawal in cases involving certain serious crimes. This creates a serious regulatory asymmetry in the Iberian Peninsula: a person rejected in Portugal may obtain access to the EU through Spain.

Spanish nationality automatically confers EU citizenship and free movement rights within the Schengen area. The contrast with Portugal’s nationality law reform raises concerns about divergent national screening standards affecting the EU’s internal security. 1.
How does the Commission assess the Schengen security impact when a Member State grants nationality to persons allegedly linked to drug trafficking, money laundering or transnational organised crime?
Will the Commission examine whether Spain’s screening procedures are compatible with loyal cooperation and Schengen security obligations?
Will the Commission propose EU-level safeguards to prevent nationality procedures from becoming an entry route for organised crime into the Schengen area?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.9.2026) According to settled case-law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, it is for each Member State, having due regard to international law, to lay down the conditions for the grant and loss of the nationality of a Member State, while its powers must be exercised having due regard to EU law1.

Where a Member State awards nationality, the person concerned automatically becomes an EU citizen in accordance with Article 9 of the Treaty on European Union2 and Article 20(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union3. EU citizens enjoy the right to move and reside within the territory of the Member States as enshrined in the EU Treaties and further regulated in Directive 2004/38/EC4.

Directive 2004/38/EC allows Member States to restrict the freedom of movement and residence of EU citizens on grounds of public policy, public security or public health, provided that the restrictive measures comply with the principle of proportionality and are based exclusively on the personal conduct of the individual concerned, which must represent a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of society.
1 Judgment of 29 April 2025, Commission v Malta (Citoyenneté par investissement), C-181/23, EU:C:2025:283,

paragraph 81 and the case-law cited. 2 Consolidated version of the Treaty on European Union. OJ C 326, 26.10.2012, pp. 13 – 45. 3 Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. OJ C 326, 26.10.2012, pp. 47– 390.

4 Directive 2004/38/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the right of citizens of the Union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States. OJ L 158, 30.4.2004, pp. 77–123, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2004/38/oj.
